primary_focus: Implement the canonical single-pass hash-map complement lookup pattern for Two Sum and stop relying on hardcoded returns/unfinished skeletons.
thinking_and_logic: The final submission does not demonstrate a Two Sum algorithm: it iterates over indices but performs no computation inside the loop and returns a constant [0, 1]. The answer key’s optimal approach is to maintain a dictionary mapping previously seen values to their indices; for each number x at index i, compute c = target - x, and if c is already in the map, return [map[c], i] (ensuring two distinct indices). This yields O(n) time and works across negatives, pairs at the end, and other common edge cases.
code_assessment: Your code contrasts sharply with the canonical solution: it has a loop skeleton but does not implement either the brute-force nested loops (O(n^2)) or the optimal hash-map single pass (O(n)). As a result, it fails 8/10 tests, including 'pair at end', 'negative numbers', and 'two elements'. The canonical approach would also prevent the known pitfall of using the same element twice by checking complements among previously seen indices (or by ensuring i != j in brute force).
